explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Micah says, "there is no cluster to eat, no early fig that I crave." He compares himself to someone gleaning a vineyard, and that gleaner comes up with no cluster. It's like reaching into the cookie box at the end of the party and feeling nothing but crumbs.

I see why the fig grabbed you, because it's right there in the verse. But Micah says there is "…no early fig that I crave." So it's not even one. That's like digging in the cookie tin for the last cookie, and the tin is bare.

explanations.answer: More fruit than he can carry
explanations.explanation: Oh, that would be a great day to be a gleaner! Arms full, big smile, maybe a little dance. Micah says the opposite, though: "there is no cluster to eat…" The prophet Micah says he's like a gleaner with no cluster and no early fig.

explanations.answer: Hunt one another with a net
explanations.explanation: Yes. Micah says, "They all lie in wait for blood; they hunt one another with a net." A net is what you'd think of for hunting animals, and here the people hunt one another. I'll say it plainly: this part is heavy.

That one sounds like it could fit, but Micah doesn't say it here. He says the people "…hunt one another with a net." Right before that, he says they lie in wait for blood. Selling people isn't in these verses.

Nope, no sheep anywhere in this passage, friend. Micah says they "…lie in wait for blood…" and "…hunt one another with a net." The ones being hunted are the people themselves. It's a heavy picture, and the text doesn't soften it.

Careful, because the word "few" isn't in there. Micah says, "They all lie in wait for blood…" He doesn't say some of them, or most of them. He says all of them, and just before that he says there is "…no one upright among men."

That's right. Micah doesn't say a few. He says, "They all lie in wait for blood; they hunt one another with a net." He says it right after he says "there is no one upright among men." It's a heavy verse, and "all" is the word it uses.

Yep. Micah says, "the prince and the judge demand a bribe." A judge is the one who's supposed to be fair, and this one has his hand out. That's a referee checking his pocket before he blows the whistle. I think that's a heavy thing to see in the leaders.
Sacrifice is a religious word, so I get the pull. But Micah never says the prince and the judge demand one. He says they "…demand a bribe." That's the picture here, nothing about the altar.

Nice try, but nobody is calling a fast in this verse. The text says, "the prince and the judge demand a bribe." Those two are the leaders of the people. Micah is pointing at them as part of the problem.

That's right. Micah says, "When the powerful utters his evil desire, they all conspire together." One powerful person speaks his evil desire, and then they all conspire together. That's exactly what the verse says.

Actually, that one is word for word what Micah says. "When the powerful utters his evil desire, they all conspire together." The powerful person speaks, and then they all conspire together. It's right there in verse 3.

You got it, friend. Micah says, "The best of them is like a brier…" A brier is a thorny bush, the kind that snags your sleeve when you walk by. So even the top of the list is prickly. Micah doesn't have one smooth, friendly option to point to.

A fig tree is good to look at, and a fig shows up in verse 1. That's the fruit Micah is hoping for, though, and he can't find it. About the best of them, he says, "The best of them is like a brier…" A brier doesn't give you figs. It gives you scratches.

The vineyard is in verse 1, so the vine makes sense. But a young vine means fruit is coming, and Micah isn't saying that. He says, "The best of them is like a brier…" A vine gives you something to eat, and a brier snags your sleeve.

Look at the tense, friend. Micah says, "The day for your watchmen has come, the day of your visitation." It's not on its way, and it's not far down the road. It has come. Then he adds, "Now is the time of their confusion."

That's right. Micah says, "The day for your watchmen has come, the day of your visitation." He doesn't say it's a long way off, because it has come. Then he says, "Now is the time of their confusion." Both of those sound like the present.

explanations.answer: The one who lies in your arms
explanations.explanation: Yes. Micah says, "Seal the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your arms." Right before that, he says not to rely on a friend or trust in a companion. Then he points to someone in your arms. It's a heavy line.

You'd expect a stranger to be the risky one, and that's what makes this verse jump out. Micah doesn't say stranger. He says "Do not rely on a friend; do not trust in a companion." Then he says to seal your mouth from "…her who lies in your arms."

Micah does talk about leaders, like the prince and the judge in verse 3. But he doesn't mention officials or a gate here. In this verse he says, "Seal the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your arms." It's about someone a lot closer than that.

That's the one. Micah says, "A man’s enemies are the members of his own household." He's been listing family: a son, a daughter, a daughter-in-law. I think this is the part of the passage that hurts most. These are the people who should be on your side, and the text says otherwise.

An army is what you'd think of for enemies, I know. But Micah says, "A man’s enemies are the members of his own household." He's not talking about an army marching in. He's talking about the people under the same roof, and that's a heavy thing to say.

Micah has been talking about the people around him, so the city makes sense. But in this verse he says, "A man’s enemies are the members of his own household." The word he uses is household, not city. Just before it, he names a son, a daughter and a daughter-in-law.

explanations.answer: Look to the LORD and wait
explanations.explanation: That's the turn, friend. Micah says, "But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation." Everyone around him is a risk, so he looks up instead of around. I think that's a big breath after a heavy passage. And he doesn't just look, he waits.

I bet a lot of us would be tempted to pack a bag after verses like these. Micah doesn't say that, though. He says, "But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation." His plan is to look and wait.

That sounds like a reasonable plan, but it's not what Micah says. Just before this he says, "Do not rely on a friend; do not trust in a companion." What he says he will do is this: "But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation."

That's right, and it's a good place to end. The last words in the passage are "My God will hear me." After all those verses about people who can't be trusted, Micah is still sure about that. He's not guessing, and he's not just hoping. He says it flat out.

I get why you might doubt it after all that heavy stuff. But look at how Micah finishes: "My God will hear me." He doesn't say "maybe," and he doesn't trail off. He ends with that. It's a firm line after a rough passage.
